That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers.

part.title: Glaciers as stores of fresh water

turns.text: Good morning, everyone. I'm Hamish Calloway, and today we're continuing our unit on the water cycle by looking at glaciers, which, as you'll see, are enormous stores of fresh water. I'll start with how they form, then look at how they release water to rivers and farms, and I'll finish with what happens when they shrink.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Right, so how does a glacier form? Lots of places get heavy snow in winter, but that alone isn't enough. For a glacier to develop, the snow has to survive the summer, so that some of it's still lying there when the next winter's snow arrives. Then it builds up, layer on layer, year after year.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: As those layers get thicker, something interesting happens underneath. The weight of the new snow presses down on the older snow, and the grains get packed closer and closer together. Over time the air between the grains is squeezed out, and what you end up with is dense, solid ice. In very cold places, that can take well over a century.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: If you've been up to Franz Josef or Fox Glacier on the West Coast, you'll have noticed that the ice often looks blue. A lot of people assume it's reflecting the sky, but that's not it. Because the ice is so dense, it absorbs the red part of sunlight, and the blue light is what's left for us to see.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Okay, so how much water are we actually talking about? You'll sometimes see three-quarters quoted, but the more accurate figure is that glaciers and ice sheets hold about 70 per cent of the world's fresh water. Now, most of that isn't in places like New Zealand, or even Iceland. It's locked up in two huge ice sheets: the one covering Antarctica, which is by far the largest, and the one on Greenland.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: But it's the smaller mountain glaciers that matter most for people, because that's the water that ends up in rivers. Some researchers call them batteries, but the term you'll see most often in the literature is water towers. The idea is that they store water high up in the mountains and let it out gradually.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: And the timing of that release is the key point. Snow and ice melt fastest in the hottest months, which tends to be exactly when there's the least rain. So glacier meltwater keeps rivers flowing during droughts, when they might otherwise drop very low or even dry up completely.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: You may also have noticed that glacial rivers are a strange milky, turquoise colour. That's caused by tiny particles of rock which the glacier grinds up as it moves over the ground. It's sometimes loosely described as silt, but geologists call this glacial flour, and it's so fine that it stays in the water for a long way downstream.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Now, let's think about who uses this water. Here in Canterbury, rivers fed partly by snow and ice from the Southern Alps, the Rakaia, for example, supply irrigation schemes right across the plains. Traditionally that land was mostly used for sheep, but these days a large share of the irrigation water goes to dairy farms, which need pasture to keep growing right through summer.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: And it's the same story, on a much bigger scale, in other parts of the world. In Central Asia, for example, rivers that start in the Pamir and Tian Shan mountains water huge areas of farmland. Some wheat is grown there, and some rice, but the crop that depends most heavily on meltwater is cotton, which needs a great deal of water in the dry growing season.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Right, so finally, what happens as glaciers shrink? Almost all mountain glaciers are getting smaller, and New Zealand's have lost a large share of their ice since the late 1960s, sorry, the late 1970s, when regular surveys began. Now, you might expect river flow to drop straight away. But a glacier that's losing ice faster than it gains it actually releases extra water, so at first, flows increase.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Eventually, though, the glacier gets so small that the amount of melt starts to fall. The point where meltwater reaches its maximum is called peak water, and after that, rivers get less every year. For many rivers in Asia and South America, scientists think that point has already passed, or will within the next twenty years or so.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: There's a second danger as well. As glaciers retreat, they often leave behind lakes held back only by piles of loose rock that the ice pushed up. If one of those natural dams gives way, the water can empty out in minutes and cause sudden, destructive floods in the valleys below.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: So, to sum up, glaciers aren't just beautiful scenery. They're a kind of savings account of water that many communities have been drawing on, and once it's spent, it isn't easily replaced. Next week we'll look at groundwater, which raises some similar questions. Okay, any questions before we finish?
turns.speaker: lecturer
